name: Ask, approve, try it
intro: A client who is not an engineer asks for a CRM dashboard in plain words, approves twice, and 17 minutes later has working, tested software waiting for review. Every frame is from a real run on a real server.
facts: Request to merge request, approvals included
Words the client typed to approve
links: The factory, and how to run it

scenes.kicker: A software factory, for people who are not engineers
scenes.title:
Ask. Approve.
Try it.
scenes.say: A client asks for software in plain words. A factory of AI agents builds it, checks it, and shows it to them.
scenes.voice: Ask. Approve. Try it. Let me show you a different way to get software built... from the client's side.

scenes.title: Sound familiar?
points: What you asked for isn't quite what gets built.
You find out at the very end, when changes cost the most.
AI writes code in seconds. But who checks it?
scenes.voice: You've probably been here. You ask for something, and what gets built isn't quite what you meant. It takes weeks, and you only find out at the very end. And now AI can write code in seconds... but who's actually checking it?

scenes.title: An assembly line for software
scenes.define: Like a car on a production line, every request moves through the same written stages. AI agents do the work at each stage, and people step in at the two moments that matter.
scenes.voice: That's where a software factory comes in. Think of an assembly line. Every request moves through the same written stages, like a car on a production line. AI agents do the work at each stage... and people step in at the two moments that really matter.

scenes.title: Every request, the same way
scenes.voice: Here's the whole pipeline. The factory reads the request and writes the requirements. You approve. Then it plans, builds, checks, and puts it online. You try it, and approve again. And then it's handed over. Agents do every step... except the two that are yours.
scenes.say: The pipeline: agents do every stage except the two that are yours

scenes.title: Checked, recorded, approved
points: A second agent verifies everything the first one built.
Every check leaves written evidence you can read.
Nothing is built, or shipped, without a person saying yes.
scenes.voice: So why should you trust it? Three reasons. Everything is checked twice: a second agent verifies whatever the first one built. Everything is recorded: every check leaves evidence you can actually read. And nothing gets built, or shipped, without a person saying yes.

scenes.title: Three parts to play
points: Asks in plain words. Approves twice. Tries the result.
Writes down the request, plans it, builds it, checks it, puts it online.
Sets the factory up once. Decides what ships.
scenes.voice: There are three parts to play. The client asks, approves, and tries the result. The factory writes it down, plans it, builds it, checks it, and puts it online. And your team sets the factory up once... and decides what ships.

scenes.title: Watch one request, start to finish
scenes.say: A client asks for a CRM dashboard. Everything you see next is real.
scenes.voice: Enough talk. Let's watch one real request, from start to finish. A client wants a CRM dashboard... and everything you're about to see actually happened.

scenes.title: Ask in plain words
scenes.say: The client has a GitLab login and a project of their own.
scenes.voice: Let's start where the client starts. Asking.

scenes.title: Start from an empty app
scenes.say: Each client gets a private project. It starts as an empty page.
scenes.voice: Every client gets a private project of their own.

scenes.say: The client's app, before the first request
scenes.voice: This is their app today. Just an empty page, waiting for its first request. And it sits behind a login only they have.

scenes.say: Their own private project in GitLab
scenes.voice: And here's their project in GitLab. This one project is all they see on the server.

scenes.title: Ask for something
scenes.say: A new issue, written the way you would message a colleague.
scenes.voice: Now, they ask for something.

scenes.say: A title, and what they want, in their own words
scenes.voice: They open a new issue. The template asks two simple questions: what should change, and how will you know it works? Here, they want a CRM dashboard, with customers in a table and totals at the top.

scenes.say: Filed. The factory label hands it over.
scenes.voice: They hit Create. The template adds the factory label... and that's what hands the request over.

scenes.title: The factory writes it down
scenes.say: Nothing is built until the client agrees with what was understood.
scenes.voice: Next, the factory writes it down.

scenes.title: It picks the request up
scenes.say: Within a minute, it says so on the issue.
scenes.voice: First, it picks the request up.

scenes.say: It reports each step on the issue as it goes
scenes.voice: Within a minute, it comments on the issue. Picked up, requirements written, and now it's waiting for a person. It reports every step like this, out in the open.

scenes.say: Its turn is over. Now it is the client's.
scenes.voice: Then it stops, and says exactly what it needs: read the requirements, and reply approve.

scenes.title: Read what it understood
scenes.say: The request, turned into stories with checks.
scenes.voice: So, what did it understand?

scenes.say: Requirements, written from the client's words
scenes.voice: An agent read the request and the code, and wrote it all down as requirements.

scenes.say: Each story comes with checks it must pass
scenes.voice: Each story comes with acceptance checks. Every later step is held to these, so the client is agreeing to something specific.

scenes.say: The status page: where it stands, and whose turn it is
scenes.voice: The client also gets a status page. Plain words, five steps, and whose turn it is. Right now, it's theirs. And one button takes them straight to the conversation.

scenes.title: Approve with one word
scenes.say: Reply approve. That is the whole interface.
scenes.voice: Approving takes one word.

scenes.say: One word starts the build
scenes.voice: They just reply: approve. And that comment kicks off the next step, right away.

scenes.title: One builds, another checks
scenes.say: A maker builds each section. A separate checker verifies it.
scenes.voice: Now the real work. Building, and checking.

scenes.title: Plan, build, check
scenes.say: Nothing moves on until a second agent says it passed.
scenes.voice: It plans, it builds, and it checks.

scenes.say: The plan: sections, each ending in a check
scenes.voice: First, a plan. The work is split into sections, and every section ends with a check that can actually be run.

scenes.say: A maker builds. A separate checker verifies.
scenes.voice: One agent, the maker, builds a section. A different agent, the checker, verifies it. The checker never saw the maker work. And if something fails, the work goes back with written notes.

scenes.say: The checker's evidence: what it ran, expected, and found
scenes.voice: The checker writes down its evidence: every check it ran, what it expected, and what it found. And that evidence travels with the change.

scenes.say: Then the whole change is checked again, and put online
scenes.voice: Then the whole change is checked again, the tests run, and it's put online for the client to try.

scenes.title: Try it before it ships
scenes.say: The client uses the real change in a browser.
scenes.voice: And now, the fun part. Trying it.

scenes.title: Use the change
scenes.say: A link to the change, running.
scenes.voice: They get to use the real thing.

scenes.say: The client's turn again, with a link to try it
scenes.voice: The factory stops again, and posts a link: Try it.

scenes.say: The status page says so too
scenes.voice: The status page says the same. Built, checked, and it's their turn.

scenes.say: The CRM dashboard they asked for, running
scenes.voice: And here it is. The CRM dashboard they asked for, running right there in the browser. Built from one short paragraph.

scenes.say: Totals at the top, every customer at a glance
scenes.voice: Totals at the top, every customer at a glance. Just what the issue asked for... and just what the requirements checked.

scenes.title: Approve again
scenes.say: Happy with it? One word again.
scenes.voice: Then, they approve again.

scenes.say: The second and last approval
scenes.voice: Happy with it? They reply approve. And that's the second, and last, thing they type.

scenes.title: Handed over, with proof
scenes.say: A merge request with the code, the tests, the specs and the evidence.
scenes.voice: Finally, the hand-over.

scenes.title: A merge request opens
scenes.say: Merging stays a person's call.
scenes.voice: A merge request opens.

scenes.say: Code, tests, specs and evidence, ready for review
scenes.voice: The factory opens a merge request, with the code, the tests, the specs, and the checker's evidence, all linked to the issue. Then someone on your team reviews it, and merges it.

scenes.say: Done. Every step ticked.
scenes.voice: The status page shows it's done. Every step ticked, with links to the conversation, the change, and the finished work.

scenes.say: The whole history stays on the issue
scenes.voice: And the whole story stays on the issue. Every step, every check, every approval, all in one place.

scenes.title: Better for everyone
points: Ask in plain words. See progress any time. Try it before it's final.
One consistent process, proof of every check, and you still decide what ships.
scenes.voice: So what does all this mean? For clients: they ask in plain words, they can see progress any time, and they try the result before it's final. For your team: one consistent process, written proof of every check... and you still decide what ships.

scenes.title: From request to review
numbers: from request to merge request, approvals included
words the client typed to approve
sections passed their checker the first time
frames mocked: all of it is real
scenes.voice: And this run, in numbers. Seventeen minutes from request to merge request, approvals included. Two words typed by the client. Four sections, and every one passed its checker the first time. And nothing you saw was mocked.
scenes.say: This run: 17 minutes, two words typed, every section passed first time

scenes.title: One factory, many clients
points: Each client sees only their own GitLab project.
Each project gets a pipeline of its own.
Previews and a status page, behind their own login.
scenes.voice: And one factory can serve lots of clients. Each one gets their own project, their own pipeline, and their own previews and status page, behind their own login.

scenes.say: Adding a client is one command
scenes.voice: Adding a new client takes one command. It creates the project, the pipeline, the login, and the links to share.

scenes.title: Ask for a project
scenes.say: Get a project of your own, file a small request, and watch it get built.
scenes.voice: Want to try it yourself? Ask for a project of your own, file a small request... and watch it get built.
